notes: Personal undertaking appeal; conditional co-surety analysis and Byblos/TCB authorities are explicit in Mance LJ's judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Cashflow finance personal undertaking: identical co-surety terms
key_facts: Capital Bank provided confidential invoice discounting to VLSI Group plc in July 1996, with personal undertakings required from director Ian Southall and finance director Peter McCaffrey.
At the signing meeting Southall and McCaffrey each signed separate undertaking documents without comparing them; McCaffrey's undertaking referred to clause 9(e) rather than clause 9(d).
After a bad debt problem in 2000 the Bank claimed about £2.8 million from Southall under clause 9(d) but could not sue McCaffrey, who had not undertaken in respect of that warranty.
The deputy judge held Southall's undertaking was conditional on McCaffrey executing identical terms or that equity should relieve Southall given common expectation of coterminous undertakings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Chancery Division dismissal of the Bank's claim against Mr Southall under his personal undertaking; cross-appeal on misrepresentation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Southall liable notwithstanding common expectation that both undertakings would be identical; no collateral condition, misrepresentation, or wider equitable relief.
enrichment.ratio: Where separate undertaking documents are prepared for separate signature, a shared expectation that they will be in identical terms does not without more imply an express or implied condition that one surety's liability depends on another signing identical terms; equity offers no wider relief than the common law in such cases, following Byblos Bank and TCB Ltd v Gray.
legal_issues: Whether Southall's undertaking was conditional on McCaffrey executing an identical undertaking
Whether equity could relieve Southall based on common expectation alone
Whether there was a material misrepresentation as to identical terms of the undertakings
Effect of clause releasing security or other surety's obligations
linked_authorities: James Graham & Co (Timber) Ltd v Southgate Sands [1986] 1 QB 80
Greer v Kettle [1938] AC 156
Byblos Bank Sal v Al-Khudhairy [1987] BCLC 232
TCB Ltd v Gray [1988] 1 All ER 108
Evans v Brembridge (1856) 25 LJ Ch 334

confidence.notes: Outcome, ratio on conditional undertakings, and equitable relief limits are clearly stated. Misrepresentation Act relief was not required on the facts.

notes: Mahajan general civil restraint order; Bhamjee principles and jurisdictional extension to county courts are central and well documented.

enrichment.short_title: Mahajan: general civil restraint order for vexatious litigant
key_facts: Mr Mahajan pursued persistent litigation against multiple defendants and court staff following an unsuccessful county court fees claim in 1999 and subsequent bankruptcy.
The Court of Appeal had already imposed a two-year extended civil restraint order in December 2003 restricting applications concerning eight named defendants.
Despite that order Mahajan brought further human rights claims against the Department of Constitutional Affairs concerning court staff and judicial acts.
The DCA applied for a wider general civil restraint order covering all courts and defendants after McKinnon J struck out further claims as devoid of merit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for a general civil restraint order in connection with Mahajan's pending application for permission to appeal McKinnon J's striking-out decision.
enrichment.outcome: General civil restraint order imposed for two years restraining applications and new proceedings in the Court of Appeal, High Court, and any county court without prior permission of designated judges; abusive correspondence restrained.
enrichment.ratio: Where a litigant's conduct is persistently vexatious across courts and subject matters, a High Court judge or the Court of Appeal on appeal may impose a general civil restraint order for up to two years protecting court processes without extinguishing access rights; such orders may extend to county courts when the nuisance warrants it.
legal_issues: Whether Mahajan qualified as a persistent and vexatious litigant requiring a general restraint order
Whether judicial acts and court staff conduct could be challenged in private law human rights proceedings
Scope of general civil restraint jurisdiction under Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2)
Whether High Court general restraint orders may include county courts
linked_authorities: Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 2) [2003] EWCA Civ 1113; [2004] 1 WLR 88
Bhamjee v Forsdick (No 1) [2003] EWCA Civ 799
Ebert v Venvil [2000] Ch 484
Jolly v Jay [2002] EWCA Civ 277
Sirros v Moore [1975] QB 118
Clark v Perks [2001] 1 WLR 17

notes: EIA screening opinion challenge; Berkeley/Richardson distinction and delegation findings are detailed in Laws LJ's judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Brighouse retail development: lawful EIA screening opinion

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Developers sought planning permission for a predominantly retail development with swimming pool on a 3.777 hectare site at redundant mills in Brighouse, Calderdale.

After call-in and inquiry the First Secretary of State granted permission in November 2002 subject to a section 106 agreement signed by other developers after Younger Homes acquired part of the site for housing.
Calderdale Council's screening opinion in August 1999, recorded in a July 2000 letter quoting officer Philip Raper, concluded EIA was not required for Schedule 2 retail development.
Younger Homes challenged the permission under section 288 alleging the screening opinion was unlawful and the Secretary of State failed to make a screening direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against Ouseley J's refusal to quash planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; valid screening opinion existed and breaches of regulations 5(5) and 20(1) did not render permission ultra vires under section 288(1)(b)(i).
enrichment.ratio: A lawfully delegated officer's written screening opinion falling within regulation 2(1) remains effective even if not sent to the applicant or placed on the register; procedural breaches of regulations 5(5) and 20(1) are section 288(1)(b)(ii) requirements and do not automatically render permission outside the Secretary of State's powers as in Berkeley.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Raper had delegated authority to adopt a screening opinion in August 1999
Whether the screening opinion was made in the name of the chief officer as required
Whether breaches of notification and register requirements invalidated the opinion
Whether planning permission should be quashed for failure to make a screening direction
linked_authorities: Berkeley v Secretary of State for the Environment [2001] 2 AC 603
Richardson v Secretary of State for the Environment [2004] 2 All ER 31
Lebus v South Cambridgeshire District Council [2002] EWCA Admin 2009; [2003] JPL 466

confidence.notes: Regulatory framework and appeal outcome are clear. Council's confused delegation evidence complicated but resolved on appeal.

notes: Struck-out adverse possession appeal reinstated; delay explained by solicitors' conduct and Woolwich v Raja principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Adverse possession appeal reinstated after unless order default
key_facts: Judge Cooke declared disputed land the property of Generay Ltd by adverse possession against Containerised Storage Company Ltd in October 2002.
Containerised Storage's application for permission to appeal was struck out in June 2003 after repeated failure to lodge compliant appeal bundles, following Master Venne's unless order.
From March 2003 McGoldricks solicitors and counsel were instructed but Mr Todd was not informed the application had been dismissed until early 2004.
Mummery LJ held delays from March 2003 were not Mr Todd's personal fault and prejudice to Generay from counsel unavailability was not a bar to reinstatement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to review and set aside Master Venne's unless order under CPR 52.16(5), reinstate struck-out permission application, and grant permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application to reinstate granted; permission to appeal granted; appellant's notice may be amended; appeal to be heard as soon as possible.
enrichment.ratio: Serious delays in complying with Court of Appeal bundle requirements caused by solicitors' conduct rather than the litigant's personal fault may justify reinstatement of a dismissed permission application where there is no relevant prejudice to the respondent; unavailability of trial counsel on appeal is an ordinary litigation risk.
legal_issues: Whether Master Venne's unless order dismissal should be set aside
Whether delay was attributable to the applicant or its professional representatives
Whether Generay suffered prejudice by loss of Mr Lewison QC as trial counsel
Whether permission to appeal should be granted on the merits
linked_authorities: Woolwich Building Society v Raja (30 July 1999, unreported)

confidence.notes: Procedural history and reinstatement reasoning are clear. Underlying adverse possession merits were only briefly addressed for permission purposes.

notes: AG Reference on Keith Ellis rape sentence; Millberry guidelines and unduly lenient threshold analysis are straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: cohabitee rape sentence not unduly lenient
key_facts: Keith Ellis, aged 43 with no relevant convictions, was convicted of raping ASB, the adult daughter of his former partner, on 20 March 2003.

Ellis and ASB had developed a consensual sexual relationship while she lived in his spare room after January 2003, but on the night of the offence he used force after she refused intercourse while both were intoxicated.
Judge Worstenholme at Leeds Crown Court sentenced Ellis to three years' imprisonment after a contested trial.
The Solicitor-General referred the sentence as unduly lenient under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney-General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 challenging a three-year sentence for rape.
enrichment.outcome: Reference dismissed; sentence lenient but not unduly lenient; Court would have imposed four years but declined to interfere bearing in mind double jeopardy.
enrichment.ratio: Following R v Millberry, cohabitee rape involving drink and limited violence may warrant a sentence below the guideline starting point; a lenient sentence is not unduly lenient where the sentencing judge evaluated the trial evidence including the complicating effect of alcohol on both parties.
legal_issues: Whether three years' imprisonment for rape was unduly lenient
Application of R v Millberry sentencing guidelines
Relevance of force, drink, and cohabitee relationship to sentence
Whether double jeopardy should prevent increase on reference
linked_authorities: R v Millberry [2003] 1 Cr App R(S) 396
R v Price [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 73
R v M (1965) 16 Cr App R(S) 770

confidence.notes: Facts, Millberry application, and non-intervention rationale are clearly stated. Victim impact evidence nuances noted but not central.

notes: Young offender rape reference; Millberry starting point and refugee background clearly addressed by Kennedy LJ.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: young refugee's rape sentence not unduly lenient
key_facts: Edmond, an 18-year-old Kosovan Albanian refugee with no prior convictions, had intercourse with a 15-year-old fostered girl after a night of heavy drinking in his bed-sit in April 2003.
The victim woke to find Edmond having sex with her, said get off, pushed him off, and later reported rape; G, a friend present earlier, was not tried.
Edmond professed no recollection of intercourse and showed no remorse; the victim had been highly intoxicated and vulnerable.
The sentencing judge imposed 12 months' detention and training order after a contested trial, using a 3 to 4 year starting point before reduction for age and circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney-General's reference under section 36 Criminal Justice Act 1988 challenging a 12-month detention and training order for rape.
enrichment.outcome: Reference dismissed; sentence lenient but not unduly lenient; sentencing judge properly balanced grave offence against youth, drunkenness, and personal history.
enrichment.ratio: Even for rape, no fixed minimum applies; where a young offender of good character commits unplanned rape during drunkenness with limited persistence after refusal, a detention and training order may be lenient yet not unduly lenient when the trial judge who heard the evidence balances vulnerability against mitigating circumstances post-Millberry.
legal_issues: Whether 12 months' DTO for rape was unduly lenient
Appropriate Millberry starting point for an 18-year-old offender
Weight of victim vulnerability, drink, and lack of remorse
Whether pre-Millberry case S supported the sentence
linked_authorities: R v Millberry [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 142
R v S (14 September 2001, unreported)

confidence.notes: Sentencing analysis and reference outcome are clear. Limited victim impact material before the trial judge noted in judgment.

notes: Solicitors' PI insurance notification duty; retainer limits and causation findings are fully reasoned by Tuckey LJ.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors not liable for failing to advise PI notification
key_facts: John Mowlem Construction sued Neil F Jones & Co as assignees of CSW, sub-contractors on a Bristol MOD project, for failing to advise notification of a threatened counterclaim to professional indemnity insurers.
CSW's finance director Mr Povey was competent in PI matters but did not notify the counterclaim before the policy expired on 12 March 1997, answering proposal questions falsely.
Solicitors were retained to pursue CSW's debt claim in arbitration; Masons warned in July 1997 that insurers should be notified after the counterclaim was served.
Insurers avoided both policies; CSW lost the arbitration with over £1 million awarded to JMC, largely unrecovered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Technology and Construction Court dismissal of negligence claim against solicitors for failure to advise PI insurance notification.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no duty to advise on insurance beyond the retainer; even if advised, judge's causation finding that Povey would not have notified was unassailable.
enrichment.ratio: A solicitor's duty is defined by the retainer; when retained only to pursue a debt claim a reasonably competent solicitor need not advise notification of a tactical counterclaim to PI insurers, especially where the client is competent in insurance; failure to notify despite broker warnings breaks the chain of causation.
legal_issues: Whether solicitors owed a duty to advise CSW to notify PI insurers of the counterclaim
Scope of retainer when counterclaim was threatened in February 1997
Whether CSW would have notified insurers if properly advised before policy expiry
Application of Midland Bank v Hett Stubbs and Credit Lyonnais v Russell Jones and Walker
linked_authorities: Midland Bank Trust Co Ltd v Hett Stubbs and Kemp [1979] 1 Ch 384
Credit Lyonnais Bank Nederland NV v Russell Jones and Walker [2002] EWHC 1310 (Ch)
Carradine Properties Ltd v DJ Freeman & Co [1999] Lloyd's Rep PN 483

confidence.notes: Liability and causation conclusions are explicit. Assignment and contributory negligence issues were not decided.

notes: Devaseelan guidelines upheld on second human rights asylum application; IAT interference with Joffe evidence analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Second human rights claim after failed asylum: Devaseelan upheld
key_facts: LD, an Algerian national, failed asylum appeal in May 1998 after self-representation when lawyers withdrew; he remained in the UK and made a fresh human rights application in 2001 under the Human Rights Act 1998.
The second adjudicator upheld the appeal relying heavily on Dr Joffe's expert report on Berber activism and post-2001 state risk, admitting it because prior representation was poor.

The Immigration Appeal Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, holding the adjudicator failed to apply Devaseelan guidelines and uncritically accepted Joffe while ignoring contrary country evidence.
New grounds alleging detention risk from counter-terrorism inquiries and Berber spring 2001 events supplemented the original fundamentalist threat case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from IAT determination allowing Secretary of State's appeal against second adjudicator's human rights decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Devaseelan guidelines valid; IAT entitled to interfere because second adjudicator failed Slimani caution and did not address contradictory country evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Devaseelan provides permissible guidance for second human rights applications after failed asylum without creating res judicata; the IAT may set aside a second adjudicator who re-litigates rejected facts without very good reason and accepts expert evidence without addressing Slimani reservations and reputable contrary material.
legal_issues: Validity and scope of Devaseelan guidelines for second human rights applications
Whether second adjudicator should have admitted and relied on Dr Joffe's report
Whether IAT erred in interfering with second adjudicator's fact-finding
Relationship between asylum persecution test and Article 3 risk
linked_authorities: Devaseelan v SSHD [2003] Imm AR 1
Slimani (01/TH/00092)
R (Bagdanavicius) v SSHD [2003] EWCA Civ 1605
Chahal v United Kingdom (1996) 23 EHRR 413
Subesh v SSHD [2004] EWCA Civ 56
A v UK [2003] EWCA Civ 175

notes: Castor fraud unless-order appeal; lengthy CPR 3.9 discretion analysis by Arden LJ with clear disposition.

enrichment.short_title: Castor fraud: default judgments on unless orders upheld
key_facts: CIBC Mellon trustees sued Wolfgang Stolzenberg and corporate defendants including Mora and Chascona over approximately CAN$240 million lost in the collapse of the Castor finance group.
Mora and Chascona, beneficially owned by hidden owner Cavazza via Gambazzi, consciously refused to comply with freezing and unless orders from 1998 onward.
Default judgments were entered after debarring orders in 1999 when disclosure and asset orders were not complied with; applications to set aside were dismissed by Etherton J in February 2003.
Cavazza's interest only emerged in 2001; applications to set aside were delayed pending the Chinablue jurisdiction application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Etherton J's refusal to set aside default judgments and related freezing and unless orders; permission refused on conspiracy issue, granted on discretion under CPR 3.9.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal on conspiracy issue refused; appeal on discretion issue dismissed; respondents' notice upheld in part; permission to appeal to House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 3.9 a party who consciously defied unless orders over years, delayed setting aside applications, failed to tender key witnesses, and offered unrealistic conditions cannot complain that a specialist judge rightly refused to set aside default judgments given serious risk to fair trial and enforcement costs prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether respondents had real prospect of success on conspiracy claim against Mora and Chascona
Whether Etherton J erred in refusing to set aside judgments under CPR 3.9
Whether a fair trial remained possible after non-compliance and document issues
Whether Cavazza's late emergence justified relief from sanctions
linked_authorities: Wytcherley v Prosser [2001] EWCA Civ 925
KJM Superbikes Ltd v Hinton [2001] EWCA Civ 1280
Paragon Finance Ltd v Nash [2001] EWCA Civ 1466

confidence.notes: Disposition and CPR 3.9 reasoning are clear in a very long judgment. Conspiracy merits were not fully decided after permission refused.

notes: Nanny entry clearance judicial review withdrawn after minister meeting offered; half costs on Scott Baker principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Veja nanny entry clearance: judicial review withdrawn
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Veja, Gujarati-origin UK residents, sought entry clearance for Miss Karavadra from India as a domestic worker nanny for their two young children.
Mrs Veja had a medical condition requiring assistance; the couple advertised locally without finding a suitable Gujarati-speaking nanny matching their cultural needs.
Entry clearance was refused on 16 January 2003 outside the immigration rules; the minister wrote on 27 March 2003 stating no compelling compassionate circumstances after promising an MP meeting.
After permission was granted the Home Office reviewed and reaffirmed refusal on 4 May 2004; shortly before hearing the minister agreed to meet the constituency MP for full reconsideration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal of entry clearance and ministerial correspondence; application withdrawn on basis of ministerial reconsideration with preserved appeal rights.
enrichment.outcome: Application withdrawn; if reconsideration fails claimants may pursue appeal with time extension; Secretary of State ordered to pay half of claimants' costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where judicial review is resolved by ministerial agreement to personal reconsideration without a concluded merits decision, costs fall to be resolved on Scott Baker Boxall principles; neither clear success nor clear failure warrants full costs, and late concession after significant delay may justify partial costs.
legal_issues: Whether minister's 27 March 2003 letter breached legitimate expectation of personal consideration
Whether refusal letters gave adequate reasons
Who should bear costs when judicial review is withdrawn after late ministerial concession
Whether compassionate circumstances justified entry clearance outside the rules
linked_authorities: Alexandrina Boxall and Brian Boxall v Mayor and Burgesses of the London Borough of Waltham Forest

confidence.notes: Procedural outcome and costs reasoning clear. Substantive compassionate grounds not finally decided; legitimate expectation issue left open.
